turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm glad you came in today. What brings you in?
turns.patient_response:
Well, hi, yeah, thanks for seeing me. I guess I'm here because... well, I've just been struggling a lot lately at work, and it's starting to really pile up on me. I'm a high school teacher, and, you know, it's a job that requires a lot of behind-the-scenes work. It’s not like I don't care about my job—I actually really love teaching, the kids are great, mostly—but the administrative side of things is just becoming impossible for me to manage. 

Like, I'll have this whole plan for my planning period or my evening at home. I'll make a cup of coffee, clear off my desk, get everything set up perfectly so I'm ready to go. I can sit down with a huge stack of student essays that I absolutely have to get through, or maybe a new curriculum document the district sent out that I need to review for the next quarter, and I fully, one hundred percent intend to just work and power through it. 

But then... I don't even know how it happens, honestly, but within ten minutes, maybe even less, I'll suddenly realize I’ve just been staring at the exact same page the entire time. My eyes are on the paper, but I'm barely taking in a single word of what's in front of me. Instead, my brain is just off in a million different directions, thinking about three or four completely unrelated things—like what I'm going to make for dinner, or remembering a random conversation I had with a colleague three days ago, or wondering if I need to get my car's oil changed soon. And by the time I snap back to reality, I haven't accomplished anything. It's just so frustrating because I *want* to do the work, I sit down to do it, but my brain just sort of unplugs from what's right in front of me.

turns.doctor_question: Did these attention problems begin when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, actually, they did. I mean, it’s not like I woke up one day in my twenties and suddenly couldn't focus. It's always been there, just... maybe it looked a little different back then, or maybe the consequences weren't as severe because, you know, when you're a kid, adults kind of manage your life for you. 

But if I really think back to primary school, I can remember it being an issue even then. My parents kept all my old report cards—my mom has this huge plastic bin in her basement with every piece of paper I ever brought home—and if you look at them, the comments from my teachers are almost identical year after year. It was always, always things like, "He's a bright boy, but he's so careless," or "He rushes through his work and makes silly mistakes." 

And the big one was always about finishing things. Every single teacher wrote some variation of "Doesn't finish his work unless closely supervised." Like, if the teacher was standing right over my shoulder, tapping the desk, I could get the math worksheet done. But the second she walked away to help someone else, I’d be staring out the window at a bird on the playground, or I’d be taking apart my mechanical pencil to see how the spring worked, and the worksheet would just sit there, half-finished. 

And then there was the whole issue with turning things in. My backpack was basically a black hole. My parents would sit me down at the kitchen table, watch me do my homework, watch me put it in my folder, watch me put the folder in my backpack... and somehow, between the kitchen table and the teacher's desk the next morning, it would just vanish from my mind. My parents were constantly finding these crumpled-up, totally completed worksheets just shoved at the bottom of my bag under a bunch of old snack wrappers weeks after they were due. I had done the work, I just... forgot to take it out of the bag. So, yeah, it’s definitely been a lifelong thing, it’s just that now, instead of a crumpled math worksheet, it’s a stack of junior year history essays, and there's no one standing over my shoulder to make sure I get them done.

turns.doctor_question: As a child or adult, did you often act impulsively or without thinking?

So, jumping into things without thinking? That’s really just not me at all. 

Even when I was younger, I wasn't the kid who was, you know, blurting out answers in the middle of class or jumping off the very top of the jungle gym without looking. I was always the quiet one, the one who was just sort of spaced out in the back row. Like I was saying earlier about those old report cards, the problem the teachers had with me was never that I was doing things recklessly or acting out of turn, it was that I wasn't doing what I was supposed to be doing because my brain was on another planet entirely.

So, yeah, acting without thinking isn't really a problem I've ever had. If anything, I think way too much, it's just... usually about the completely wrong things at the wrong time.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often interrupt people or blurt out answers before they finish speaking?
turns.patient_response:
No, definitely not. I'm actually really careful about that, probably because, well, as a teacher, I see it all the time and I know how disruptive it can be. You know, you're in the middle of trying to explain the causes of the French Revolution, and you've got this whole narrative arc built up, and you're just getting to the Storming of the Bastille, and suddenly a kid just shouts out, "Wait, did they have guillotines yet?!" And it's like, okay, great question, I appreciate the enthusiasm, but you just completely derailed the entire train of thought for the other twenty-nine kids in the room. 

So because I'm so hyper-aware of how that feels from the front of the classroom, I'm really, really conscious of not doing it to other people. If I'm in a conversation, I'm usually the one who's maybe a little too quiet, just waiting for a very clear, obvious pause before I jump in. And honestly, half the time, by the time that pause actually happens, I've completely forgotten what I was going to say anyway because my brain drifted off while I was waiting. 

Like, my girlfriend and I will be talking about, I don't know, where to go for dinner, and she'll be listing off places, and I'll have a thought about this one Thai place we went to a year ago, but I don't want to interrupt her list. So I'll just hold onto that thought, but then while I'm holding onto it, I start thinking about how we haven't had Thai food in a while, and then I wonder if there's a difference between red curry and green curry, and by the time she finally stops talking and asks what I think, I'm sitting there wondering how they harvest bamboo shoots and I have absolutely no idea what she just said to me. So, yeah, blurting things out isn't really my issue. I'm much more likely to just fade out of the conversation entirely while the other person is still talking.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had a hard time waiting your turn?
turns.patient_response:
No, I can't really say that I have. I know a lot of people get incredibly frustrated with that kind of thing, but for me, waiting is honestly just... it's almost like a free pass to check out for a few minutes. I don't get antsy at all.

She'll be sighing, shifting her weight, looking around for another lane to jump into. But me? I'm completely fine. I'll just stand there, staring at the rack of chewing gum or the tabloid headlines, but not even really reading them, you know? Just completely lost in my own thoughts.

You've got all these teachers who are highly caffeinated and stressed out, tapping their feet, checking their watches every five seconds because the bell is going to ring. I'll start thinking about how I'm going to explain the themes in *To Kill a Mockingbird* that afternoon, or I'll remember a documentary I watched three years ago about deep-sea marine life, and suddenly fifteen minutes have gone by and I haven't even noticed that I've just been standing there doing absolutely nothing. 

So, no, the whole "waiting your turn" thing has never been a struggle. I don't feel that urge to push ahead or interrupt people. If anything, people probably have to remind me that it *is* my turn because I've completely forgotten that I was even waiting in a line to begin with. I'll just be standing at the deli counter, miles away in my own head, until the guy behind the counter has called my number three times and the person behind me has to nudge my shoulder. So yeah, definitely not an issue with impatience or jumping the gun. I'm perfectly content to just stand there and be in my own little world.

turns.doctor_question: As an adult, do you often feel the need to move around or fidget when you’re supposed to sit still?
turns.patient_response:
No, not really. I mean, it’s kind of like what I was saying about when I was a kid. The physical restlessness just isn't there for me at all. 

Like, as a teacher, we have these professional development days a few times a year, right? And they are notoriously grueling. They usually stick all the staff in the cafeteria or the auditorium, sitting on those terrible, hard plastic folding chairs that haven't been replaced since the nineties, and we have to listen to a guest speaker talk about, I don't know, standardized testing metrics or new curriculum mapping software for like three hours straight. 

And if you look around the room during one of those sessions, you can see all the other adults practically crawling out of their skin. The math teacher next to me will be furiously clicking his pen, the history teacher in front of me will be bouncing her leg up and down so hard the whole row of chairs shakes, and people are constantly getting up to go to the bathroom or get more coffee just to have an excuse to move their bodies. 

But me? I am completely planted. I don't feel that physical itch to get up and pace or stretch my legs. I can sit in that incredibly uncomfortable plastic chair for the entire three hours without so much as shifting my weight. Now, am I actually listening to the presentation? No, probably not. My mind is usually off somewhere completely different. I'll be sitting perfectly still, looking right at the speaker, but internally I'm trying to remember if I took the chicken out of the freezer to thaw, or I'm mentally rewriting a lesson plan on *The Great Gatsby*, or I'm just zoning out completely, thinking about what kind of car I'd buy if I won the lottery. 

But physically? No, there’s no fidgeting. No tapping, no squirming. It's actually kind of a problem sometimes, because I get so still and so quiet that my principal probably thinks I'm paying incredibly close attention, and then later she'll reference something from the meeting and I'll have absolutely no idea what she's talking about because I wasn't present at all. But yeah, the physical need to move around... I just don't get that. My body is perfectly happy just staying in one spot for hours on end, even if my brain has left the building.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often feel restless inside, even if you stay physically still?
turns.patient_response:
No, I wouldn't use the word restless. I know I said earlier that my mind goes a million miles an hour, but it's not... it's not an uncomfortable feeling, if that makes sense? 

When I hear the word "restless," I think of feeling trapped, or having this pent-up energy that has nowhere to go, like you're just itching to break out of your own skin. I really don't get that at all. It’s actually funny you ask that, because we just had midterms a few weeks ago. And when you're proctoring a midterm exam for tenth graders, the district rules are incredibly strict. You can't grade papers, you can't read a book, you can't be on your computer or looking at your phone. You literally just have to sit at the desk at the front of the room and watch thirty teenagers take a test for two straight hours. And the silence in the room is just... it's heavy, you know? The only sound is the clock ticking on the wall and maybe some kid aggressively erasing a scantron bubble. 

The other teachers in the department complain about it constantly. We'll be in the breakroom and they'll talk about how proctoring is literal torture, how they feel like they're going crazy inside their own heads, just mentally begging for the bell to ring because they feel so agitated and pent-up just sitting there with their own thoughts. 

But for me? I honestly kind of look forward to it. It’s not agonizing at all. I don't feel that internal tension or that desperation for it to be over. My mind just sort of... detaches and floats off. I’ll spend the whole two hours mentally redesigning my living room, or trying to remember the starting lineup of the 1998 Chicago Bulls, or just playing out these incredibly elaborate, hypothetical scenarios in my head. I'm not fighting some internal urge to escape, and I'm not feeling anxious or restless inside. I'm just comfortably, completely spaced out. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I feel restless on the inside either. It's never a feeling of being trapped or agitated. It's really more like my brain just takes the opportunity to go on a very long, very meandering vacation while my body stays behind.

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly denies feeling restless on the inside, stating they do not feel trapped or agitated.

turns.doctor_question: Do you currently have any of the hyperactive or impulsive symptoms, like difficulty staying seated, fidgeting, or blurting things out?
turns.patient_response:
No, honestly, I really don't. I know we kind of just touched on the fidgeting and the internal restlessness a second ago, but yeah, even looking at the whole picture—the staying seated, the blurting things out, all of that—it's just... it's really not me. I don't have any of that hyper energy. 

Like, with staying seated, for example. We have these parent-teacher conferences twice a year, and they set us up in the main gymnasium, which always smells vaguely of floor wax and old sweat. It's just rows and rows of these little folding tables, and we are expected to sit there from 4:00 PM to 8:00 PM as the parents cycle through. And some of the other teachers, I mean, they literally cannot handle it. You watch them and they're standing up, stretching their backs, walking over to the water fountain every ten minutes, leaning against the bleachers just to change positions. But I will literally sit in that exact same spot, in that same posture, for the entire four hours. I don't even think about getting up. My body just sort of... powers down, I guess? 

And then as for the blurting things out or being impulsive... no, definitely not. If anything, I probably have the exact opposite problem. Like, when I'm leading a class discussion—say we're talking about the symbolism of the green light in *Gatsby*, which we usually do right around November—the kids will be talking, and I'll be listening, but then my brain will just snag on something one of them said. And I'll start following this long mental thread about the American Dream, or the history of the 1920s, or I'll wonder if Fitzgerald actually intended for it to mean all that or if English teachers are just over-analyzing it. And suddenly there's this huge, awkward dead air in the room because I haven't responded to the student who just spoke. 

I never interrupt them. I never just blurt out the answer or talk over people. I'm usually so deep in my own head that I'm the last person to speak up in a conversation, whether that's in the classroom or, you know, at a dinner party with my wife's friends. I'll just be sitting there, perfectly still, while they debate where to go for dinner, and I won't say a word because I'm thinking about something completely unrelated. So, yeah, I don't have that impulse to jump in or interrupt or jump out of my seat at all. It's just not how I operate.
